standard.title: Identity shaped by language and culture
standard.description: recognise how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values
standard.prior_knowledge: Students enter the Y7-10 sequence without formal prior study of target language cultures. They bring lived experience of identity shaped by their own language(s) and cultural contexts, but have not yet examined how language and culture interact to shape identity in the target language community or reflected on how learning the target language affects their own sense of identity.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — in target language communities and in their own experience — and identify specific language features, cultural practices and texts that reflect and reinforce identity.

nodes.label: Language and cultural identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify ways in which the target language reflects and reinforces cultural identity, attitudes and values.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language features or cultural practices in the target language community that reflect shared values or identity (e.g. forms of address, naming conventions, greeting customs).
nodes.typical_width: Examine a range of target language features — forms of address, naming conventions, cultural references in language, regional variations — and discuss how each reflects or reinforces aspects of cultural identity; compare with English-language conventions.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian languages encode connections to Country, place and community — compare with how the target language encodes connection to place or community
Research regional identity within the target language community — identify language differences that reflect regional, national or community identity and discuss what they signal

response_modes.reason: Students need encounter with a range of cultural contexts where language and identity intersect before the connection becomes generalisable. Single examples (e.g. one greeting convention) tend to be treated as curiosities rather than patterns. Varied cultural encounters build the repertoire from which the general insight emerges.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Examining how different languages encode cultural values and identity is the foundational insight of the Languages curriculum's intercultural dimension. At Y7-8, concrete and varied examples make this conceptually accessible while building the framework that deepens across Y9-10.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two target language features or cultural practices that reflect cultural identity or values
Can compare at least one of these with an equivalent or contrasting English-language convention

nodes.label: Register, context and social identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise how language use varies according to social context, relationship and identity, and identify examples in the target language.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of how language use in the target language changes based on social relationship, context or purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Examine how register, formality and language choice reflect and reinforce social relationships in the target language; identify culturally specific behaviours and expressions that signal social identity; compare with Australian English conventions.
wider: Examine culturally embedded expressions or terms of address in the target language that encode social relationships not equivalently expressed in English
Investigate how multilingualism shapes identity in target language communities — interview or research bilingual speakers' experiences of moving between languages and identities

response_modes.reason: Students need scaffolded discussion to move from observing a language variation ('they say it differently to the teacher') to understanding the social mechanism behind it ('this reflects a social relationship structure that the language encodes'). Explicit discussion prompts and cultural context explanations support this move.

success_criteria: Can identify at least one example of language use in the target language that reflects a social relationship or context
Can explain the social or cultural reason for the language choice with reference to the target language community

nodes.label: Personal identity and language learning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can reflect on how their own identity is expressed through language and consider how learning the target language affects or expands their sense of identity.
nodes.minimum_width: Articulate at least one way in which their own identity is expressed through their language use; reflect on at least one way in which learning the target language has introduced a new perspective.
nodes.typical_width: Reflect on the connections between language and personal identity in their own experience; explore how values, beliefs and attitudes are carried in language choices; consider how acquiring the target language creates a new lens through which to view their own and others' worlds.
wider: Create a personal text (slogan, visual, short reflection) in the target language that expresses an aspect of their own identity — discuss the choices made and what was translatable or not
Interview a multilingual person about their experience of identity across languages — compare insights with own reflections on the language learning experience

response_modes.reason: Personal identity reflection integrates the cultural and social insights from nodes 1–2 with the student's own experience. The teaching investment is in creating genuine reflective opportunities — not just asking students to describe themselves, but to examine the role language plays in how they are seen and how they see others.

success_criteria: Can articulate at least one connection between their own language use and their personal identity
Can identify at least one new perspective introduced by learning the target language and explain why it is new
